Android shows hardware buttons only to an accessibility service, so KeySnap uses one for exactly that: noticing a press and running your shortcut. It does not read other apps\' screens. During Advanced Mode setup it also reads the pairing code on the Wireless Debugging page, and nothing else.
Android closes apps it thinks are idle, and a closed app cannot run your shortcuts. This keeps KeySnap alive while your phone sleeps. In the background it does nothing but wait for a button.

Open source · nothing leaves your phone
This stops Advanced Mode, deletes the bridge from the device, and removes every shortcut and preference. It cannot be undone. The Accessibility service switches off too; turn it on again afterwards.
Nothing you do here leaves your phone.
No servers. No account. No analytics. KeySnap has nowhere to send your shortcuts or your key presses — and the whole app is open source, so you don\'t have to take our word for it.

KeySnap has no backend, no account and no crash reporting. What you map, what you press and which apps you use stay in this app\'s private storage. There is no code in it that uploads any of that, because there is nowhere for it to go.
Open source, so you can check
Every line of KeySnap is published under the GPLv3. Read what each permission is used for, build it yourself, or hand it to someone who can.
The accessibility service only sees Settings

Android gives apps no other way to detect a hardware key. KeySnap\'s service is locked to the system Settings app and uses it for exactly one thing: reading the pairing code while you set up Advanced Mode. It cannot read your bank app, your messages, or anything you type — that is enforced by Android, not by a promise.
Advanced Mode is your own phone\'s ADB

It pairs with your phone\'s own Wireless Debugging over your local network — that connection never leaves your home. It runs shell commands only for the shortcuts you wrote. Switch it off and the helper is deleted; a reboot stops it too.
